II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00332

That covenant gives earthly life its meaning in Islamic spirituality: life is the test of whether we remain faithful to the promise made with God before time began. The prophets come to remind people of that earlier promise.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00333

But what exactly does it mean, and how can we keep it? The answer is a secret hidden beneath the outward wording of the revelations brought by the prophets. This is why the verse has inspired so much reflection in the tradition of inner spiritual knowledge known as irfan, or gnosis. Such knowledge has always troubled strict interpreters of religious texts and defenders of fixed doctrines. It reveals a level of reality and awareness that they do not accept. And it is knowledge that saves and transforms: it cannot come into being without a process of spiritual initiation and renewal through which a person's deeper self awakens.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00334

From this point of view, a human being is not primarily a sinner, sick with an inherited original sin. A human being is an exile—a gharib (see Book II, Chapter V, and Book III, Chapter I)—whose task is to understand why they are far from home and how they can return. Those who refuse the return lose themselves in a hopeless abyss. Those who seek the way home find it through inner knowledge: by discovering the hidden meaning of the prophetic revelations through ta'wil, the practice of leading their outward words back to their spiritual meaning. This is what makes spiritual rebirth (wiladat ruhaniya) possible.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00335

The need to find both the path and a guide for travelling it lies at the very roots of Shiism. It is also where prophetic philosophy begins. Its spirit could hardly be expressed better than in an image used by the great philosopher Mulla Sadra of Shiraz (d. 1050/1640): “The Qur'anic revelation is the light by which we see, like the sun pouring out its light. Philosophical understanding is the eye that sees that light. Without the light, nothing can be seen.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00336

“But if we shut our eyes—that is, if we claim we can do without philosophical understanding—the light itself will go unseen, because there are no eyes open to receive it.” The apparent conflict between philosophy and theology is overcome from the outset in hikmat ilahiya, or “divine wisdom.” By Mulla Sadra's time, this prophetic wisdom would come to mean, above all, the spiritual interpretation of the Qur'an taught by the Imams.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00337

Revelation and philosophical reflection are thus bound together from the beginning. Philosophy, when understood as prophetic philosophy, cannot be separated from spiritual effort or personal spiritual fulfilment.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00338

We can already see a basic difference between this approach and an understanding of Islam centred on religious law. The law-centred understanding of Sunni Islam and the inner spiritual teaching of Shiite Islam start from the same belief but draw different conclusions from it. Both accept that Muhammad brought the earlier cycles of prophecy to a close. Before him came the great prophets—Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus. Muhammad was the last prophet to bring a revealed religious law, or sharia: the Seal of the prophets who give laws (nubuwwat al-tashri).
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00339

Now suppose prophetic revelations have only their outward, literal meaning. Suppose they amount to nothing beyond a moral and social law. In that case, humanity's religious history has truly come to an end, because there will never be another divinely revealed sharia. We have already heard the Fifth and Sixth Imams declare that if the Qur'an had no meaning beyond its literal words, it would already be dead.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00340

But suppose the text of revelation contains something hidden, something the Prophet, in his role as prophet, was not charged with disclosing (see Chapter VI). Everything changes. Then religious life becomes a waiting for the full meaning of revelation to be revealed at the end of time. That unveiling advances through what Corbin calls the night of hidden meaning. The night began with the First Imam, after the Prophet left this world. It will end only when the last Imam, the Twelfth, who is now hidden, finally appears. His appearance will herald the Great Resurrection (al-Qiyamat al-Kubra).
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00341

For Shiism, teachings about the end of time are not merely a vague article of faith or a way to encourage moral behaviour. They are fundamental to its philosophy. A prophetic philosophy is inseparable from an understanding of the last things: it arises from an awareness of what is to come and gives shape to the ways people anticipate it. Perhaps nearly everyone in Islam could agree with the arguments by which the Shiite Imams, from the beginning, explained why prophets were necessary.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00342

But what happens after the last prophet has come, now that no more prophets will appear? This is the urgent question that Shiism raises and seeks to answer. Indeed, prophetic philosophy is needed precisely because there will be no more prophets.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00343

The answer is the walayat of the Imams, which continues after the last Prophet's risalat, his mission of bringing God's message. This is the answer given in the traditions attributed to the Imams themselves. It is also developed by leading Shiite thinkers devoted to divine wisdom, such as Ibn Abi Jumhur (who died after 901/1496). For these writers, what chiefly sets Shiism apart from mainstream Islam is walayat: the Imams' spiritual bond with God and their role as guides to the hidden truth. This is the inner reality of religion—the res esoterica, literally “the hidden matter” (al-amr al-batina). The Islam understood through Shiite spiritual awareness therefore calls for initiation into a teaching that leads to salvation. In this sense, it is a form of spiritual knowledge within Islam.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00344

At its heart is a claim that was enough, from the very beginning, to alarm the scholars of Sunni orthodoxy, in its concern for religion's literal forms. Everything outward, everything visible, every surface appearance (zahir) has an inward, hidden reality (batin). The outward is the form in which the inward becomes visible: the place where it appears (mazhar). And the reverse is equally true: every inward reality requires an outward form. The outward is what we can see of the inward; the inward is its spiritual truth, its real nature (haqiqat), its secret, its inner knowledge, and its meaning beyond the senses (ma'na). The outward takes shape in the visible world. The inward has its reality in the unseen spiritual world (alam al-ghayb).
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00345

This relationship between outward form and inner reality is reflected in the relationship between the Prophet's mission as God's Messenger (risalat) and the Imam's spiritual mission as a Friend of God (wali Allah). The Prophet brings about the “descent” (tanzil) of revelation: its arrival in the world in the form of words and religious teachings. For Shiism, this necessarily calls for another, complementary task: to lead those revealed words back to their spiritual truth, their original meaning. That return is ta'wil. Its literal sense is “leading back,” and it names the spiritual interpretation of revelation.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00346

This work belongs above all to the Imam's special spiritual gift and guiding role—his walayat. Just as the outward and inward meanings depend on each other, prophecy and the Imam's work of spiritual guidance (nubuwwat and walayat) are interdependent and inseparable. The Shiite understanding of the Imam can therefore exist and make sense only within the spiritual awareness that gives rise to it. It is a basic, guiding image in religious consciousness—one that comes before any evidence drawn from outward experience.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00347

Any other explanation would miss what fundamentally distinguishes Shiite belief in the Imams from mainstream Islam understood chiefly as a religion of law, with its concern for the validity of actions and rituals and its suspicion of attempts to uncover an inner dimension through spiritual initiation. Equally, to discuss inner spiritual traditions in Islam while leaving out Shiism—as Western scholars have often done—is to miss something essential. It ignores the claim that faith (iman) reaches its full meaning only through the Imam's walayat: by recognizing both the Imam's identity and his spiritual role.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00348

Faith also needs ta'wil, an inward understanding (ma'rifat) of divine revelation (see Chapter V). From a Shiite perspective, separating spiritual interpretation from the doctrine of the Imams would amount to turning Shiism into something detached from its own sacred foundation. As we shall see, this becomes especially important when we examine the relationship between Shiism, Shiite Sufism, and forms of Sufism that do not identify themselves as Shiite.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00349

We have already introduced several key ideas about prophecy and the role of the Imams. We will examine them more fully in Chapters V–VII. But a few more points are needed now, especially those that our authors use to describe the Imam's spiritual identity. The Friend of God's guiding role—his walayat—is directed towards knowing the inner meaning of divine revelation. In contrast, the ordinary inheritance left by a prophet (warathat) concerns the outward meaning, the words of revelation as they stand.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00350

We will see in Chapter VI, section 4, what is involved in inheriting spiritual knowledge. The Imam's role in its fullness includes both outward and inward knowledge. To receive the Prophet's spiritual trust (wasayat) is to preserve the continuing line of inner meaning (silsilat al-batin). The worldly caliphate, or outward succession to the Prophet, preserves the line of outward religious law and teaching. But without the inner line, its claim to preserve that inheritance is always uncertain and open to question.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00351

This distinction already shows why the question of the Shiite Imamate is far greater than accounts that reduce Shiism to politics or struggles for power. Ali ibn Abi Talib, the First Imam and the Prophet's cousin and son-in-law, became only the fourth caliph in the official history of Islam's outward institutions.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00352

But that does not lessen his standing as Imam. Nor does the earlier position of the first three caliphs—Abu Bakr, Umar, and Uthman—give them the spiritual authority of an Imam. Neither does holding the caliphate give that authority to later Umayyad or Abbasid rulers. To understand what is at stake in Shiism is to understand that it is not simply a matter of supporting one political dynasty against another. The Imam does not need to be recognized by the general population in order to be Imam. His spiritual gift is invisible to them, as is the spiritual world from which it comes and to which it belongs. His status therefore does not depend on their judgment.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00353

There are even times when the Imamate must remain hidden—as it does during the present period of ghaybat, the Imam's concealment. The worldly caliphate concerns the maintenance of the sharia, the outward inheritance. None of the eleven Imams who came after Ali actually exercised that caliphate.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00354

Yet each was still the Guardian of the Holy Book (Qayyim al-Qur'an). This means something very different from political rule. It is the caliphate in its “true sense,” realized in the person of the Imam. But its complete realization belongs, by its very nature, to the fulfilment of history at the end of time.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00355

A passage that captures the spirit of Shiism especially well will now bring these ideas together. It records something like the closing words of a conversation between the Sixth Imam, Jafar al-Sadiq, and one of his closest disciples, Mufaddal ibn Umar al-Jufi. This is how Mufaddal himself tells the story:
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00356

“Our cause is difficult,” the Imam said. “To bear it, people need minds in which the dawn can break, hearts burning with light, healthy souls, and beautiful natures. God has already received the pledge (mithaq) of our Shiite followers. May God faithfully grant paradise to whoever remains faithful and loyal to us. Whoever betrays us and violates our right has already placed himself in hell.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00357
“God has entrusted us, the Imams, with a secret—a secret whose burden He placed on no one else. Then He ordered us to pass it on, and we do.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00358

“But we would have found no one worthy of receiving it, no one able to hold and carry it, if God had not created certain people for that purpose. They were formed from the clay of Muhammad and his descendants—from the very substance of the Prophet and the Imams. They were created from the light of the Imams through the overflowing generosity of divine mercy.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00359

“We pass on to them what God has commanded us to pass on. They welcome it and can bear it; their hearts are not disturbed. Their spirits are in harmony with our secret. They are naturally drawn to a spiritual understanding of who we are, and of their own accord they seek to know our cause.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00360

“But God has also created people who belong to hell. We have been ordered to tell them the same thing, and so we tell them. Yet their hearts close against our secret. They recoil from it, throw it back at us, and deny it as false because they cannot bear it. God has placed a seal upon their hearts. Their tongues speak a portion of the truth and repeat its words, but their hearts reject it.”
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00361

Then, Mufaddal relates, the Imam wept. Raising both hands, he prayed: “O my God, let them live as we live and die as we die! Do not let an enemy prevail over them. For if You allowed their enemies to overcome them, there would be no one left in this world to worship You.”
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00362

This passage, so strongly marked by the Shiite spiritual outlook, will echo throughout the pages that follow. It prepares us for the interpretation of Qur'an 33:72 as a verse concealing the secret of the trust God placed in humanity. It also expresses themes found in the First Imam's conversation with his disciple Kumayl ibn Ziyad (see Chapter III, sections 2 and 3). It suggests that, in the scene of the covenant before time (mithaq), the yes spoken by humanity did not come from every heart in the same way.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00363

Some hearts already concealed a refusal. Their owners would be the enduring deniers, people whose initiation never came to completion, whose answer was a no disguised as a yes. Their destiny, too, would spring from a choice made before earthly life—one that no human explanation can fully reach.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00364

Finally, the Imam's opening statement matches the beginning of a famous tradition identifying the Imams' secret with the secret of interpreting revelation's hidden meaning. It therefore points towards the mystery of the Primordial Prophetic Reality (Haqiqat Muhammadiya; see Chapter V).
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00365

We can now identify two further points that complete the Twelver Shiite understanding of the Imamate. First, why do the Imams form a complete group of twelve persons sharing one spiritual reality, and how do they perform an essential role in revealing God even before appearing on earth? Second, why does this role make the Imamate a necessary part of the eternal religion of prophecy, present throughout every period of the prophetic cycle?
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
en-book-1-ch-2-s3
3. The Complete Circle of the Twelve Imams
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00366

To understand these two points, we must first consider why the number twelve is held to be complete in itself. The Prophet's reported statements about the number of Imams are taken as proof of that completeness. Because the group of twelve forms a perfect whole—a pleroma, or complete circle—its number cannot be exceeded. That is what gives the mysterious Twelfth Imam his special place.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00367

We must then consider how this pattern appears throughout the universe and throughout sacred history. The Twelve are made manifest at different levels in the coming-into-being of the cosmos and during the successive periods of prophecy. These many forms of manifestation surround the earthly lives of the historical Imams, whose appearances were brief and took place during the first three centuries of Islam.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00368

The number twelve also matters in Seven-Imam Shiism, or Ismailism. There, however, it does not specify a fixed total number of Imams. Rather, it refers to the twelve dignitaries, or hujjats, who permanently surround each Imam. So twelve does not establish quite the same basic pattern in the two branches of Shiism. This is an important difference. Many traditions state that the Imams number twelve, some attributing this teaching to the Prophet and others to individual Imams.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00369

To show why twelve represents a perfect and complete whole, these traditions point to the twelve signs of the zodiac, the twelve princes or tribes of Israel, the twelve springs that appeared when Moses struck the rock, the twelve months of the year, the twelve hours of the day, and other examples. In this way, Twelver Shiism takes up an entire theology of the Aeon: a sacred order of time and cosmic completeness.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00370

The Imamate also has its origin in the eternal Prophetic Reality (Haqiqat Muhammadiya), before and beyond all its appearances in our world. That is why the relationship between the Prophet and the Imam—between Muhammad and Ali ibn Abi Talib—is unique. With the Prophet of Islam, the Imamate was openly revealed.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00371

But it had already been “revealed in secret” alongside each of the earlier prophets who brought religious laws, as we shall see. The prophets' chief mission had always been risalat: delivering the divine message in its outward, literal form. The Imams' task was to guide people into the hidden spiritual meaning of that revelation through ta'wil and tahqiq, the search for its true reality. They lead people towards spiritual understanding. More than that, they are themselves that inner meaning (see Chapter V).
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00372

This is because Shiite reflection on the Imams sees their existence before earthly life as the first manifestation of God: a heavenly reality beyond ordinary humanity, created rather than divine in itself, but serving as the Face through which God becomes known to human beings. People turn towards that Face when they turn towards God, because God in His own being remains inaccessible to them: the unfathomable depth, the divine Silence, the hidden God (Deus absconditus). This idea of the divine Face is central to Shiite theology. It is not the result of later speculation; it is already expressed in sayings attributed to the Imams themselves.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00373
We shall see in Chapter VII that the Imam, understood in this way, makes it possible for human beings to know God's oneness (tawhid).
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00374

However hard we try, we can turn only towards the Face of God as revealed (Deus revelatus). By recognizing this, we avoid two opposite errors: tashbih, making God resemble a human being or other created things, and ta'til, treating God as so unknowable that we are left with no living knowledge of Him. From this Shiite standpoint, anyone who rejects the Imam repeats the error of Iblis. One path leads to tashbih, a misunderstanding of God's names and attributes; the other leads to ta'til, which tries to protect God's absolute otherness but merely replaces a naïve, human-like picture of God with an abstract one.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00375

The Twelve Imams, together with the Prophet and his daughter Fatima—Fatima al-Zahra, “the Radiant,” “she who shines like flowers,” and the mother of the Imams' line—form the complete circle of the Fourteen Pure Ones (Chahardeh Ma'sum in Persian). Their manifestations, or appearances through which God becomes known, take place at different levels of the universe: lahut, jabarut, malakut, and nasut (see Chapter V).
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00376
We cannot explore all the comparisons here, for they need fuller study. But the group has striking similarities to groups of twelve and fourteen found in Coptic Gnostic texts.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00377

The Apocalypse of Adam, for example, speaks of fourteen Aeons of light, forms in which the Illuminator appears. In Shiite language, we might call them the visible forms (mazahir) of the eternal Prophetic Reality. Manichaean spiritual teaching interprets a prayer offered by Seth, Adam's son, to the “fourteen great Aeons of light.” Seth, as the “Imam of Adam,” is also an important figure in Shiite inner teaching.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00378

The same Manichaean tradition speaks of the “fourteen vessels” on which Jesus travelled down into this world. The likeness between the Twelfth Imam—the fourteenth of the Pure Ones—and the fourteenth Aeon of light is especially striking. In the Apocalypse of Adam, the fourteenth is a stranger, a being from elsewhere: a boy born under mysterious circumstances, carried away to a place no one can reach, and brought up and nourished there.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00379

The Twelfth Imam, Muhammad al-Qa'im (“the One Who Will Rise”) or al-Mahdi (“the Rightly Guided”), is also said to have been born mysteriously. He disappears while still a child, on the very day his young father, the Imam Hasan Askari, leaves this world (260 AH/873 CE; see Book VII).
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00380
We shall hear the Prophet Muhammad speak of him in words recalling those of the prophet Zarathustra about the saving figure called the Saoshyant: “I am in him, and he is in me.”
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00381

The Twelfth Imam, the fourteenth of the Pure Ones, is the Hidden Imam of our own age. According to this understanding, he lives in a world beyond the senses, invisible to human beings, until his future appearance brings the present cycle of the world to an end. The time in which we live is the time of his concealment, the ghaybat. As the Imam who is awaited (Imam muntazar), he has been identified by several Shiite writers, including Haydar Amoli, with the Paraclete whom Jesus promises in the Gospel of John.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00382

We shall return to this, because the connection between the Shiite understanding of Islam and the promised Paraclete raises an important question for a wider study of the world's religions—a field of thought that may yet develop in the future. Since devotion to the Twelfth Imam lies at the heart of Twelver Shiism, the final book of this work will be devoted to him. For the same reason, we could not go any further without introducing him here.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00383

As we have said, numerous Shiite traditions, or hadiths, are cited in support of the complete group of twelve. Shiite interpreters also find support in Qur'anic verses, while a cosmic understanding of divine wisdom reveals further patterns that we will consider later. Here we can do no more than touch on a few of the many traditions.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00384

In one tradition, the Prophet declares: “There will be twelve Imams after me. The first is Ali ibn Abi Talib; the twelfth is the One Who Will Rise (al-Qa'im), the Mahdi—the Rightly Guided, and therefore himself the Guide (al-Hadi). Through him, God will bring the East and West of the earth under His rule.” Other traditions compare their number to the months of the year, the springs that Moses brought from the rock at Horeb, or the chiefs (nuqaba) of Israel.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00385

Addressing Ali, his own spiritual successor (wasi), the Prophet says: “Ali, the Imams, rightly guided and guiding others, your descendants who are perfectly pure, will be twelve in number, counting you among them. You are the first. The last will bear my own name, Muhammad. When he appears, he will fill the earth with justice and harmony, just as it is now filled with wrongdoing and violence.”
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00386

Another tradition recalls what the Prophet was shown during the ecstatic night of his ascent to heaven. He saw twelve lights on the supports of the Throne. Within each light was a line of green writing bearing the name of one of the twelve Imams. The same image returns in the story of an emerald tablet brought down from heaven by the angel Gabriel to Fatima Zahra, or brought to the Prophet and given by him to his daughter. We might remember here the emerald tablet of the Hermetic tradition.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00387

Written on Fatima's tablet in letters of gold that shone like sunlight were the names of the Prophet and his twelve Imams. One of the Prophet's Companions, Jabir al-Ansari, who was among the earliest Shiites, was even allowed by Fatima to copy it. The Fifth Imam, Muhammad al-Baqir (d. around 115/733), is said to have confirmed the account. In the sacred narrative, then, this testimony was given well before the line of twelve Imams had reached its historical end.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00388

These many traditions develop and explain what Shiism sees in the Qur'anic verses it regards as divine confirmation of its beliefs. Two connected ideas are especially important. The first is ismat, the purity and freedom from fault granted to the Imams by God. The second is nass, God's designation of the Imam, which means that his spiritual place cannot be assigned or taken away through human election. Two Qur'anic verses are particularly significant here.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00389

The first is Qur'an 3:54, in the verse numbering Corbin uses, which refers to the challenge known as mubahala. Muhammad offered this solemn test to the Christians of Najran and their bishop in 10 AH/631 CE. Each side would call upon God to give a sign settling their disagreement about who Christ was. As is well known, the Christians ultimately declined to take the test.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00390

But the scene prepared for it was extraordinary. On the “red dune,” the Prophet had a large piece of black cloth hung between two trees trimmed to form posts, creating a kind of canopy. He stood beneath it with his daughter Fatima—al-Zahra, “the Radiant,” also called al-Batul, “the Virgin”—behind him. On his right stood her husband and cousin, Ali, the First Imam. On his left stood the two young Imams, Hasan and Husayn.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00391

These four members of his family, together with the Prophet himself, were the five people he put forward as participants in the sacred test. Together they are known as the Five People of the Cloak (Ashab al-Kisa). This is the same cloak that the Hidden Imam will wear when he appears, giving the image a remarkable power. Shiite belief understands these five people, joined by a sacred bond, as a manifestation of God. For Shiite theologians, the Qur'anic wording leaves no doubt that the Five share one essence (ousia), one spiritual reality (haqiqat).
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00392

Another verse makes the same five people sacred, and through them the succession of Imams down to the Twelfth. It is not descent by blood alone that makes each of the Twelve an Imam. What matters is ismat, purity granted by God, together with nass, God's explicit designation of that person. Qur'an 33:33 says: “God wishes to remove all impurity from you, members of the Prophet's household, and to make you entirely pure.” Again, the five are gathered under the Prophet's cloak. On this occasion he prays: “My God, these are the members of my house. My brother Ali is the prince of the Imams, his sons are the finest of my descendants, and my daughter is the sovereign of women. The Mahdi will come from our family.”
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00393

One of the Companions, again Jabir al-Ansari, asks: “Messenger of God, who is the Mahdi?” The Prophet replies: “There will be nine Imams descended from Husayn. The ninth will be the Qa'im, the One Who Will Rise. He will fill the earth with harmony and justice, just as it is now filled with tyranny and violence. He will struggle to bring people back to the spiritual meaning (ta'wil), just as I struggled to reveal the outward words (tanzil).”
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00394

That final sentence explains why, as we shall see at the end of this work, the Twelfth Imam stands at the centre of the whole cycle of spiritual initiation—the cycle of walayat—that began when the cycle of prophecy came to a close. Here we meet a paradox that is characteristic of Shiite thought and is already present in the Prophet's statement that twelve Imams would succeed him. How can twelve be enough to cover all the time remaining until Yawm al-Qiyamat, the Day of Resurrection? From the beginning, the line of twelve Imams cannot be compared with, or set in competition against, any worldly dynasty. It belongs to another order of reality.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00395

On the one hand, the earth can never be without an Imam, even an invisible, hidden one. Without him, the earth would lose its connection with heaven. The Imam is its spiritual centre; if he ceased to exist, humanity could not continue to exist. Whether the great majority of people know of this centre or not makes no difference. The Imam must therefore always be present.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00396

On the other hand, the complete circle of twelve is already established. Twelve is the perfect number: fewer would leave the Imamate incomplete, and more would break the very completeness that gives it meaning. The Twelfth Imam must therefore exist now, and must have existed in this world from the moment the Eleventh Imam departed it.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00397

Yet the cycle of spiritual guidance through walayat is not over. The Twelfth Imam's final appearance is still awaited. He must therefore be both already present and still to come—someone who has existed in the past and whose appearance belongs to the future.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00398

This double relationship to time defines his existence today. It is a presence between times: invisible and enduring, from the beginning of his “Minor Occultation” in 260 AH/874 CE until the end of historical time and the dawn of a new Aeon, the age of the Perfect Human Being. Such a presence cannot be an ordinary physical presence at a location in the visible world. It requires another world, beyond the senses, between the world we know and the highest spiritual reality, with its own kind of time (see Chapter IV, section 5). This lasting presence is what makes the idea of a Hidden Imam necessary, along with the doctrine of concealment, or ghaybat.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00399

Shiite thinkers devoted to divine wisdom have reflected on it at great length. It protects the central idea of Twelver Shiism from being reduced to a worldly institution or a political and social programme (see the whole of Book VII).
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00400

Besides the verses of the Qur'an and the teachings attributed to the Prophet and the Imams, Shiite doctrine is supported by a larger vision of how the universe came to be and how sacred history unfolds. Within Shiism, these ideas preserve a much older tradition of inner spiritual knowledge. Unlike what happened in the West, philosophical thought here was not confined by a more or less arbitrary boundary between inherited religious teaching and speculative reasoning.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00401

The only aim worthy of such thought was a complete understanding of divine wisdom, a theosophia in its fullest sense. Qur'anic verses and traditions provide material for thinking about the universe. In return, philosophical accounts of the universe continually refer back to those sacred sources. Their meeting reveals the second great feature of the Imamate mentioned earlier: its place as an essential part of a universal religion of prophecy, present throughout every period of the prophetic cycle.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00402

Consider, for instance, a saying attributed to the Sixth Imam, Jafar al-Sadiq: “Night has twelve hours, day has twelve hours, and the year has twelve months. The Imams number twelve, and Ali is one hour among the twelve.” Our authors have no difficulty seeing this as a reference to the cycle of spiritual initiation, or walayat, whose length and stages correspond to those of a cosmic day and night.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00403

In another tradition, the Prophet recites Qur'an 85:1: “By the heaven with its twelve fortified mansions”—the signs of the zodiac. Then he asks his listener: “Do you think God Most High is swearing by the astronomical sky and its constellations? The heaven spoken of here is my own person. And the twelve fortified mansions, the twelve zodiacal signs, are the twelve Imams who will come after me.”
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00404

Here the doctrine of the Imams reaches beyond earthly life to the scale of the universe itself. As we have seen, the historical persons of the twelve Imams are understood as earthly manifestations of the spiritual powers through which the cosmos comes into being.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00405

Shiite divine wisdom is therefore, at its heart, a teaching about how God becomes manifest. This is why Shiite thinkers so readily recognized ideas they saw as originally their own in the immense writings of Ibn Arabi, and made his work part of their own tradition. They did, however, refine his account of the oneness of being (wahdat al-wujud). The Shiite commentators on Ibn Arabi, especially Haydar Amoli, offer a revealing example. Haydar was quite willing to criticize teachings of Ibn Arabi that conflicted with Shiite doctrine, above all the identity of the “Seal of the walayat” (see Book IV, Chapter I).
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00406

Yet the central idea on both sides remains the same: the different levels of the universe correspond perfectly with one another, linking visible worlds with spiritual worlds. That is why the twelve Imams, from the first to the last, are said to make manifest every religion and every perfection, both spiritually and visibly.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00407

This statement by Ibn Abi Jumhur comes from a view of the universe in which the different levels of existence form a very complex order. That order also determines the different levels of meaning that spiritual interpretation uncovers in the Qur'an (see Chapter V). Let us reduce this picture to its simplest outlines, leaving aside the variations between accounts.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00408

At the eternal origin of all manifestations of God stand twelve heavenly princes, or primordial Imams. They occupy the highest heaven of twelve dwelling places, each seated on his own throne. They know the secrets of the Preserved Tablet (Lawh Mahfuz), not because they have learned them from elsewhere, but because this knowledge belongs to their very being. In their turn, they establish seven representatives or leaders (nuqaba), corresponding to the ruling Intelligences of the planetary spheres described by philosophers. These seven leaders are assisted by guardians or “temple-keepers” (sadana), some of whose roles correspond to the heavenly souls (animae caelestes) that philosophers say move the spheres.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00409

This entire order revolves in service to the twelve original heavenly princes. Twelve orders of angels serve as messengers between the worlds and correspond to them. Angels, stars, and heavens all appear as different manifestations (mazahir) of the one reality of the Primordial Human Being (Insan, the Anthropos). This primordial human reality is the source of everything that exists. Under its different names, it is the first being brought into existence by the God who forever remains beyond existence itself.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00410

If we consider the twelve heavenly Imams in their original role in the creation of the universe, angels and heavenly spirits become the forms through which they are made manifest in their respective worlds. But if we consider the Imams as they appear in human form on earth, their spirits receive inspiration and higher knowledge from those angelic spirits.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00411

In short, the worlds together are many different manifestations of a single primordial reality, which appears on earth in the Fourteen Pure Ones: the twelve Imams, the Prophet, and Fatima, his daughter and the source of their family line.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00412

The correspondences are easy to see within this traditional picture of the cosmos. The order and completeness of the visible worlds depend on the seven heavenly bodies, the seven heavens, and the twelve zodiacal constellations. The order and completeness of the spiritual cosmos are governed by the seven central figures, or poles (aqtab), who are prophets, and the twelve Imams. The spiritual orders described in Sufism have their origin in this pattern. It also helps us understand the role of the Twelve in both the cycle of prophecy and the cycle of spiritual initiation.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00413

By this same pattern of correspondence, each prophet who was not only a nabi but also a messenger (nabi mursal), sent to reveal the Book of a new religion and begin a new period of prophecy, was followed by twelve Imams, his spiritual heirs (awsiya). Each messenger was a manifestation of the same prophetic reality that finally appeared in its fullness in the “Seal of the Prophets.” In the same way, the Imams belonging to the different prophets were manifestations of one and the same reality of the Imamate. They were not reincarnations of one another.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00414

Speaking of Ali, his own direct spiritual successor, the Prophet Muhammad is reported to have said: “Ali was sent secretly with every prophet; with me he was sent openly.” The saying speaks through the person of Ali of an eternal Imam. If we remember that the Imam's spiritual role is to lead people into the hidden meaning of revelation, we can begin to see the importance of another fact: Ismaili spiritual teaching gives this “eternal Imam” the name of Melchizedek. This shows how deeply the Shiite understanding of the Imam is rooted in the idea of a universal religion of prophecy. Here we can see that idea unfolding, although the chain by which it reached the all-embracing inner vision of Shiism—one that takes in the whole of sacred history—is still far from clear.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00415

There are seven great prophets among the messengers (nabi mursal): Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, David, Jesus, and Muhammad. Their number corresponds to the seven planetary spheres. In this scheme, the seven are called the poles. Just as the movements of the planets are marked out against the heavens of the twelve zodiacal signs, the seven periods of prophecy, each beginning with one of these figures, are marked by twelve successive spiritual heirs (awsiya), or Imams.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00416

No prophet dies without appointing a spiritual successor. That successor does not take over the office of prophet; he carries on the work of the Imamate. Adam appointed his son Seth; Noah appointed his son Shem; Abraham appointed Ishmael; Moses, after Aaron's death, appointed Joshua; and Jesus appointed Shamun al-Safa, or Simon Peter.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00417

But Muhammad reminded his followers that every one of these prophets had been betrayed by his own people. He also warned that his own community would betray its promise of loyalty to the man he named as his spiritual heir, Ali ibn Abi Talib. This painful picture has a powerful place in Shiite consciousness. It is how the tradition understands what it sees as the great failure of the Sunni majority: abandoning the Imamate, which Shiism regards as the heart of Islam understood as a spiritual religion.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00418
We have already seen how difficult it is to translate the full meaning of awliya, the “Friends of God,” and walayat.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00419

We shall meet the difficulty again. A great Twelver Shiite Sufi master of the seventh/thirteenth century, Sad al-Din Hamuyah (d. 650/1252), explains that these terms appeared only with the religion of Muhammad, although the spiritual role they name had existed throughout the earlier periods of prophecy. In those earlier times, people who held this role were still called nabis, prophets in a more general sense, rather than messengers sent with a revealed Book. We shall return to these distinctions in Chapter VI, section 2.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00420

This teaching implies that with Islam—and, in this understanding, with Shiite Islam in particular—the inner meaning of religion reached its full expression. It is also the meaning given to the following saying when applied to the twelve Imams: “The sages of my community correspond to the prophets of Israel.” Our authors can name in detail the twelve spiritual guides who marked the successive stages of each earlier prophetic period.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00421

But this is one of the most difficult subjects in Shiite accounts of prophecy and the Imams, whether Twelver or Ismaili. The lists include both biblical and non-biblical names. Their sources still need careful investigation, and the rendering of many names into Arabic has changed them so much that identification is often uncertain.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00422

Among the Imams associated with Adam's period, for example, we recognize Seth, Abel, and Enoch. In Noah's period we find Shem, Arpachshad, and Japheth, as well as the Arabian prophets Salih and Hud, who are named in the Qur'an. In Abraham's period the names include Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Job, Zeno, and Daniel the Elder. For Moses, they include Aaron, Joshua, and Uzayr. For David, Solomon and Asaph.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00423

In the time of Jesus, the line begins with Shamun al-Safa (Simon bar Kepha, or Peter) and ends—through a series of names different from those of the canonical Christian group—with Bahira, also called George. He is presented as the Nestorian monk who assured Muhammad that his calling to prophecy and his visions were genuine, after Muhammad, troubled by doubt, was brought to him by his wife Khadija.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00424

This repeated appearance of the complete group of twelve throughout sacred history is essential to understanding the story of the Twelfth Imam. It is a continuing spiritual pattern, not a belief in reincarnation. It helps explain the prophetic dreams said to have been given to the Twelfth Imam's mother while she was still a Christian. The twelve “Imams of Christ” do not have quite the same role as the twelve Apostles in Christianity. They do not live at the same time. Instead, they hand on the message from one generation to the next until a new prophet is called—the last Prophet.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00425
We shall encounter them again in the story of the visionary betrothal of the Eleventh Imam and Princess Nargis (see Book VII).
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00426

Finally, we come to the Twelve Imams belonging to Muhammad's period. The Second and Third Imams are brothers, both sons of the First Imam and Fatima. From the Fourth Imam onward, the line passes from father to son. According to Shiite tradition, all died as martyrs. From the Fourth Imam on, the means of killing them is consistently said to have been poison.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00427

I. Ali al-Murtada, Amir al-Muminin (“Commander of the Faithful”), husband of Fatima and cousin of the Prophet. Born in Mecca between 600 and 605 CE; assassinated at Kufa in 40 AH/661 CE. His shrine is at Najaf.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00428
II. al-Hasan al-Mujtaba (“the Chosen One”). Born in Medina in 3 AH/624 CE and died there in 49/669. His grave is in al-Baqi, the cemetery of Medina; Baqi means “a place thick with trees.”
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00429

III. al-Husayn, Sayyid al-Shuhada (“Prince of the Martyrs”). Born in Medina in 4/625; killed as a martyr in the tragedy of Karbala in 61/680. His tomb is at the shrine of Karbala, which, together with Najaf, is among the chief places of Shiite pilgrimage. As we have already seen, he and his brother Hasan were still young boys when they joined the Five People of the Cloak. They were then called “the princes of the young people of paradise.”
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00430

IV. Ali Zayn al-Abidin al-Sajjad (“Ornament of the Devout,” “He Who Is Constantly at Worship”). Born in Medina in 36 or 38 AH/656 or 659 CE; died in the same city in 92 or 95/711 or 714. His grave is in al-Baqi. He is credited with a work of spiritual teaching known as the “Psalter and Gospel of the Prophet's Family.” Shiite writers have produced many commentaries on it, and it has remained a book of everyday devotion among pious Shiites.
